units: a mould is shaped in clay before the pouring
the molten metal is poured without a break
the piece cools for a whole night without being moved
the mould is broken once the metal has cooled
the surface looks reddish and unpolished when the shell comes off
a tuning specialist adjusts the pitch at the end of the process
material is taken away from the inside to change the note
the craftsman leaves a mark of his own when the result satisfies him
text: Long before any metal moves, the workshop grows hot. The founder builds up a clay mould by hand, layer on layer and without haste, then leaves it to dry beside the furnace. Once the alloy runs, he tips it in one unbroken stream and watches the bubbles rise across the surface. Cooling takes a whole night through; nobody lifts the piece or shifts it until it has gone lukewarm. Breaking out comes next. The shell splits under a mallet and uncovers a reddish flank, unpolished and still rough to the touch. The tuner has the last word. He strikes the rim, listens hard, scrapes fine shavings from the inside, then strikes again. Every pass lifts the note a shade higher. When the tone rings clean and the ringing dies away without a beat, he sets down his tool and cuts a small mark of his own into the metal.

units: shared places have grown too noisy
shops play music to hold on to their customers
machines about the house give out unpleasant beeps
each emission taken on its own seems harmless
it is the adding up of the sources that makes the din
attention comes apart and talking together costs more effort
vulnerable people now keep away from public spaces
doctors report a lasting exhaustion in those exposed to it
the writer holds that an individual answer would be useless
the writer asks those who build and those who manufacture to protect quiet
text: A quiet change deserves a moment of attention: the places we share have grown far too loud, and the fault belongs to no one in particular. Shops pipe out music chosen to hold customers on the floor a little longer. Machines about the house mark every task they finish with a shrill beep. Taken one at a time, each of these seems harmless enough; laid over one another, they build a din that nobody ever chose. Attention comes apart, talking together costs more effort, and the frailest users withdraw from public spaces. Clinicians report a lasting exhaustion among those who cannot step away from the noise. Since the cause is collective, no private remedy will serve: blocking one's ears merely shifts the burden along. It falls to those who design our buildings and those who make our machines to treat quiet as a resource.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she began her trade in a country workshop
her first speciality was mending cracked soundboards
the mended bodies gave out a muffled sound
neither the wood nor the varnish nor the strings explained the fault
she put the blame on a layer of glue laid on too thickly
she tested hanging samples that she tapped
the least glued samples sounded better
she changed her preparation and put right the instruments already delivered
she passes the method on to pupils who come from far away
text: The woman who restores old instruments learned her trade in a country workshop, where cracked soundboards made up most of the work. One puzzle held her for whole seasons: every body she glued back together came out muffled, as though a blanket lay over it. The wood was sound, the varnish untouched, the strings at their proper tension. In the end she turned on the glue itself, laid on too thickly, holding back the movement of the board. To test the idea she made up samples, hung each one from a thread and tapped it gently. The heavily coated pieces answered with a dull thud; the lighter ones rang out. So she thinned her layer, warmed the mixture with care and went back over every instrument she had already handed on. Her customers heard the change at the first playing. She now teaches the method to apprentices who travel a long way for it.

units: the narrator compared two recorded versions of the same set of pieces
the two hearings were a week apart
the first group takes a fast and very confident pace
this first version ends up wearing the listener out
the second group slows down and blends the colours more
a passage of the fast version is out of tune between two instruments
a piece of the slow version loses its coherence
the narrator picks the second version
his reason is that it stands up to repeated hearings
text: I sat down with two recordings of the same set of string pieces, a week between them, and the gap between the two took me aback. The first group plays fast, with a dazzling confidence: the attacks snap, and you can hear the players breathe. Brilliant, yes, though wearing after a while, a brightness nobody could keep up with. The second group takes its time. Tempos stretch, colours melt together, and what sounded angular turns round and soft. The first record grabbed me; this one kept me. Neither is faultless. Among the quick players a middle passage tips into sourness, the viola and the cello never quite agreeing. Among the slow ones, a single piece sags and loses the thread. Asked which one I would keep, I do not hesitate: the second, because it survives another hearing, and another, without going stale before the end.

units: the writer is staying in a rented house beside an estuary
he chooses to relate the sounds rather than the scenery
the water strikes the supports of the building at regular intervals
the boats scrape when the level rises
a bird lets out an evening cry that he takes for a creaking door
human noises come from the quay and from a radio set
the wooden frame creaks during the night
those creaks make up a kind of tune
the writer notes down what he observes with the hour and the wind
he means to let his recordings be heard when he returns
text: I am writing from the low house we have taken by the estuary, and rather than the view I want to give you the sounds. Water comes first: a steady slap against the piles, then the scrape of hulls as the tide lifts them and sets them nudging. Birds are second. One of them lets out a thin cry at dusk that I still mistake for a door in need of oil. Third comes everything human, voices carrying up from the quay, a radio playing somewhere out of sight, a trolley rumbling over planks. The fourth caught me unawares. The timber frame itself creaks after dark, and those creaks fall into something close to a tune. All of it goes into a notebook, with the hour and the quarter the wind blows from. When I am home again I shall play you the recordings that came out well; most beat any postcard.

units: the origin of the phenomenon is older than the keeper's memory
her grandmother already knew this echo
the first returning sound she caught seemed weakened to her
she put the cause down to the wind at first
she then suspected the work of water on the rock
a rock specialist explained to her the part played by the shape of the land
she accepts that explanation without giving up her listening
the curious go away pleased once they have shouted
she waits until she is alone to say one short sentence
the voice that comes back to her sounds lower and altered
text: When did the cliff begin to answer? The keeper of the path waves the question away: it was answering long before she was born, and before her grandmother, who knew it as a girl. What did she hear on her first night up there? A call that came back to her weakened, as though the stone were reluctant to give it up. Did she look for a reason? She blamed the wind at first, then the water that eats into the face, until a passing rock specialist spoke to her of the curve of the hollow. What does she make of that answer? She keeps it, and climbs up alone at dusk all the same to hear her own voice returned to her. And the curious? They shout, they laugh, they go away pleased. She waits for them to drift off, then says one short sentence, and the wall hands it back a little lower, a little changed, and she goes down telling nobody.

units: the technical manager explained to the performer where the shrill noise came from
the microphone was picking up the sound leaving the speakers
that sound fed back into the circuit and built up on its own
the performer believed the sound level alone was to blame
the technician answered that the aim of the microphone weighed more
he advised moving the speakers behind the performer
he suggested cutting the top frequencies and the input level
he recommended never aiming the microphone at a speaker
the trial worked apart from a brief moment during a lean towards the audience
text: The stage manager took the singer aside to tell her where the whistle was coming from. Her microphone, he said, was hearing the speakers set out in front of her; that sound went back down the line into the amplifier and built on itself until it howled. She supposed the volume was to blame. Not chiefly, he told her: which way the capsule faces weighs more, since a microphone aimed at a loudspeaker listens to its own echo. She asked what could be done. Put the speakers behind you, he suggested, pull down the top frequencies, which run away first, and take a little off the input. He added a rule for the stage: never swing the microphone round towards a source, not even while taking a bow. She tried it through the sound check. The whistle stayed away, apart from one second, when she leaned out over the hall.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: spoken transmission of melodies wore down from one singer to the next
learning was done by copying a sung model
after three handings on two neighbouring groups sang differently
the first copyists set signs above the sung words
those signs showed the direction of the voice but not the gap between the notes
it was still necessary to know the tune in order to read those signs
the solution was to rule guide lines
the height of the sign on the page then showed the pitch of the note
a performer could from then on sing a piece he had never heard
that invention opened the way to writing for several voices
text: Handing a melody from one generation to the next raised a difficulty that memory alone could not settle. Singers learned by copying what they heard, and every copy drifted a little from its model; three relays on, two neighbouring communities no longer sang the same tune. Early copyists tried marks placed above the words, recalling where the voice rose and where it fell, though never how far. The help was real but partial: you had to know the melody already before the marks meant anything. What broke the deadlock was a plain graphic idea. Rule one line across the page, then a second, and set each mark at a measurable height. From that moment the page itself stood for pitch. A singer could work out a tune he had never heard, and music written for several voices at once became possible.

units: in air the widely spaced particles pass the vibration on badly
sound weakens quickly as it travels through air
in water the closely packed particles pass the vibration on without delay
the vibration travels markedly faster in water than in air
a swimmer under the surface cannot place where an engine noise comes from
that confusion comes from the signal reaching both ears too close together
metal carries the vibration better still than water
a wall of wool damps the vibration almost entirely
the same blow gives a different sound according to the material
text: Take two ways of carrying a sound over a distance. In air the wave spreads and fades: the molecules sit well apart, they hand the shake on lazily, and the message has worn thin after a short stretch. In water those same molecules all but touch. The shake passes straight from one to the next with nothing lost between, and it travels far quicker there than it ever does in air. That is why a swimmer below the surface hears a distant engine yet cannot tell where it lies: the signal reaches both ears too nearly at once for him to compare them. Solids belong in the comparison as well. A steel bar carries the tremor better still than water, while a partition of wool soaks up almost all of it. One blow, three materials, three answers: a bright clatter from the metal, a dull ring under water, a short flat thud in the wool.

units: the narrator expected a long session but not a failed one
the injured pianist had to play with one hand only
the borrowed room belonged to a dance school
its floor threw the sounds back strongly
the singer had a cold and a ragged voice
she refused to lighten her part in spite of her state
noisy building work disturbed a quiet passage
the group carried on regardless out of stubbornness
the final result turned out to be satisfying
the musicians kept those choices for the performance
text: They warned me the rehearsal would run long. Nobody warned me it would turn into a run of disasters. First blow: the pianist turns up with a bandaged finger and announces he will manage with the left hand. Second blow: the room, lent to us by a dance school, has a floor that throws everything back, so the smallest note cracks and returns doubled. Third blow: the singer has caught a cold, her voice comes out ragged, and she will not lighten her part by a single line. Fourth and finest: someone starts drilling through the party wall during the quietest passage. We kept going out of sheer stubbornness. And the thing stood up: the left hand laid down a rocking bass none of us had imagined, the ragged voice suited the words, and the ringing floor made us play softer than we ever had. On the night we asked for rugs and kept every one of those choices.
